title: Occupancy-adaptive burst absorber and soft-degradation pathways
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Summary:
We need a tenant-aware, occupancy-adaptive mechanism that absorbs transient traffic bursts at the edge of the serving mesh and gracefully degrades outputs when sustained pressure threatens SLOs. This ticket implements a lightweight 'burst absorber' (ephemeral buffer + leak scheduler) combined with a deterministic soft-degradation pipeline and circuit-breaker integration for multi-region failover scenarios. The goal is to reduce customer-visible errors and p99 latency spikes without wholesale request dropping or expensive autoscaling for short lived spikes.

Background and motivation:
- We observe short, high-amplitude spikes from a small fraction of tenants that cause downstream queues to inflate and SLO burn for other tenants in the same pool.
- Autoscaling is effective for long tail load but slow for spikes and costly when overprovisioned.
- Existing admission controllers can drop or hard-throttle; we want a gentler path that preserves developer experience while protecting fleet SLOs.

Design overview:
1) Edge burst absorber (per-tenant ephemeral reservoir):
   - Lightweight in-memory queue co-located with the edge routing tier (per-region).
   - Configurable per-tenant occupancy limit (bytes and request count) and time-to-live (TTL) per entry.
   - Backpressure policy: if absorber occupancy < fast-path threshold, forward immediately. If above threshold but below hard-cap, queue and schedule. If above hard-cap, reject with soft-degrade fallback.
   - Leak scheduler: proportional leak rate tuned by recent capacity and latency SLO signals; favors low-latency slices when possible.

2) Soft-degradation pathways (ordered by fidelity/cost):
   - Path A (minimal): respond with truncated completion + placeholder metadata (keeps latency low, useful for chat-like UIs where partial text is OK).
   - Path B (medium): route to a distilled/quantized model variant with reduced token budget and token-sampling adjustments.
   - Path C (async): ack with 202 and schedule execution on lower-priority queue with callback/webhook to tenant.
   - Fallback policy maps tenant SLAs and request type to the chosen pathway; operators can override per-tenant.

3) Circuit-breaker integration and multi-region coordination:
   - Circuit-breaker opens for a tenant at region-level when error/latency burn exceeds threshold for N minutes.
   - When opened, traffic for that tenant is diverted to a remote region (if configured) and/or to soft-degrade paths to avoid overload.
   - Circuit state is replicated to controls plane for visibility; region-level decisions respect cross-region bandwidth limits.

4) Observability and control surface:
   - Console knobs per-tenant: absorber capacity, leak-rate multiplier, degrade-policy override, circuit-breaker thresholds.
   - Metrics exported: absorber_occupancy{tenant,region}, absorber_drops{reason}, degrade_path_taken{tenant,region}, circuit_state_changes, p50/p95/p99 latency before/after absorber.

Rollout and safety:
- Feature gated behind a tenant-level flag; initially opt-in for a small set of high-burst tenants.
- Canary in single region for 48h with synthetic spike tests and real-traffic dark launches.
- Gradual ramp to 10%/25%/50%/100% tenants per region with automated rollback on SLO burn or error-rate regressions.

Acceptance criteria:
- Implementation exists in edge routing tier with documented knobs in Console.
- In perf tests, transient 5x spike (30s) results in <= 10% increase in p99 for co-located tenants compared to baseline, and no more than 0.5% absolute increase in 30d SLO burn rate for the region.
- At least two soft-degrade pathways functional and configurable per tenant.
- Circuit-breaker correctly opens/closes per thresholds and multi-region diversion works in failover test.
- Unit/ integration tests for buffer correctness, TTL, leak scheduling, and policy mapping.

Implementation plan (milestones):
- M1 (2w): detailed design doc + API knobs + metrics contract (owner: Marco).
- M2 (3w): edge absorber proto (in-memory) + basic leak scheduler + unit tests.
- M3 (2w): integrate soft-degrade handlers (A/B/C) and Console controls.
- M4 (2w): circuit-breaker hooks + multi-region diversion wiring.
- M5 (2w): perf validation, chaos testing, canary rollout.

Open questions / trade-offs:
- Where to persist absorber state for short lived failover (memory-only vs. ephemeral replicated state)? Memory-only is fastest but harder to failover; small replication increases complexity.
- How to guarantee fairness across tenants during sustained spikes (simple proportional shares vs. credit-based dewpoint)?
- Cost of supporting async 202 workflow for many tenants (storage & retry).

- Confluence design draft: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/RELI/occupancy-adaptive-burst-absorber
- Perf dashboard (staging): https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/edge/absorber-spike-tests
acceptance_criteria:
- Edge absorber implemented and feature-flagged per tenant.
- Two or more soft-degrade pathways active and toggleable from Console.
- Canary test results: <10% p99 uplift for co-tenants under controlled 30s spikes.
- Circuit-breaker reroute succeeds in multi-region failover drill.
- Metrics emitted and dashboards created.
- PR reviewed and merged with unit/integration tests.
comments: 2026-02-18 - Design review: PM (Svetlana) requested explicit mapping table between request types (chat, embeddings, rerank) and degradation path; added to design doc.

2026-03-05 - Perf prototype results (staging): absorber reduced immediate rejects by ~72% for synthetic 10x bursts; observed small tail amplification when leak-rate set too low. Follow-up: add adaptive leak multiplier based on recent p99 latency.
2026-03-09 - PR opened: https://github.com/redwood-inference/aegis/pull/842 (edge-absorber-proto). Marked WIP pending integration tests.
2026-03-12 - PM approval to proceed with canary after adding an automated rollback that triggers on >0.3% SLO burn over 1h. Added to rollout plan.
